papers.title: Plug and schedule: scalable and modular architecture for integrated and dynamic scheduling based on graph neural networks and reinforcement learning
papers.abstract: Manufacturing companies increasingly require scheduling approaches that integrate practical constraints such as workforce availability, maintenance, setup dependencies, energy objectives, and uncertainty, yet existing research offers limited support for transferring them into heterogeneous industrial data landscapes. This paper proposes a scalable and modular architecture for integrated and dynamic scheduling that combines an Asset Administration Shell-based middleware for standardised data integration, a heterogeneous graph representation of scheduling instances, a graph neural network-based State Modeler, and a Proximal Policy Optimisation-based RL-Scheduler coupled with event-based simulation. The architecture is validated on the production system of a German machinery manufacturer with 59 manufacturing resources and 39 employees and on public benchmark instances. On the industrial instances, the learned policy reduces the makespan against the mean of seven dispatching baselines by 2.93% to 6.76% across six evaluation cells covering small-part, large-part, and combined production under deterministic and stochastic machine failures, with statistical significance in every scenario. The energy-aware configuration preserves this makespan performance while significantly reducing the relative energy cost in most scenarios. The findings indicate that the proposed architecture provides a practically transferable pathway for configurable RL-based scheduling in heterogeneous production environments.

papers.title: Impact of privacy-preserving horizontal retailer information sharing on the bullwhip effect in supply chains with multiple retailers
institutions: Vienna University of Economics and Business
papers.abstract: Experiences from real-world supply chains as well as exhaustive research show that the lack of coordination within supply chains leads to bullwhip effect, in which the magnitude of fluctuations in orders increases in the upstream direction from retailer to the supplier. One potential solution for addressing this phenomenon is information sharing between supply chain actors that can reduce the impact of fluctuations in customer demand on the supply chain. However, sharing too much information might lead to higher vulnerability of stakeholders in negotiations with their partners or to an unwanted leakage of information to competitors. Therefore, relevant actors are often reluctant to share the necessary information. To overcome these problems, we propose a horizontal information sharing model where retailers share demand information in form of average values between each other without revealing the exact values of each individual partner. This could be achieved by, e.g., applying costly cryptographic methods. Therefore, we evaluate the potential effects of this type of information sharing on the whole supply chain by developing a simulation model representing a 4-echelon supply chain, which consists of multiple customers, each served by their own retailer, one wholesaler, one manufacturer and one supplier. We investigate the effect of horizontal information sharing of average customer demand among the retailers on the bullwhip effect and show its effects on the different supply chain actors. In addition, the influences of demand variability and demand correlations between customers, different forecasting methods, safety stock approaches, stochastic lead times and the number of retailers sharing the information on the bullwhip effect are analyzed.

papers.title: Balancing and scheduling of transfer lines for cycle time and peak power minimisation: a learning-enhanced multi-objective variable neighbourhood search
papers.abstract: As global electricity demand surges due to industrial electrification and digitalisation, peak power (PP) management has emerged as a critical challenge in energy-intensive manufacturing, affecting operational costs and grid capacity. PP is defined as the maximum instantaneous total power demand across all workstations during the production cycle, and its minimisation is essential for reducing demand charges and avoiding grid overloads. This study introduces the balancing and scheduling of machining transfer lines as a bi-objective optimisation problem that simultaneously minimises cycle time (CT) and PP under precedence, inclusion/exclusion, and technological compatibility constraints. A multi-objective constraint programming (CP) model is formulated and solved via a bidirectional ε-constraint method, generating high-quality Pareto sets for small-scale instances. To overcome the computational intractability of CP for medium- and large-scale problems, a multi-objective variable neighbourhood search (MOVNS) enhanced with deep reinforcement learning (NN_MOVNS) is proposed, in which a Deep Q-Network adaptively guides neighbourhood operator selection throughout the search. Computational experiments on 55 benchmark instances demonstrate that NN_MOVNS consistently outperforms competing algorithms across all problem scales, with improvements becoming increasingly pronounced on larger instances, as confirmed by statistical significance tests. Peak shaving experiments confirm PP reductions ranging from 33% to 73% with modest CT increases averaging 5.7%. An industrial-scale test instance of a 148-task automotive cylinder head production line achieves an 11.8% CT reduction and a 63.1% PP reduction, lowering the peak-to-average power ratio from 2.35 to 1.49.

papers.title: Mitigating supply chain transparency barriers with blockchain: a dynamic capabilities perspective
papers.abstract: The complexity and risk uncertainty stemming from supply disruptions underscore the need for enhanced transparency in supply chain management. Although blockchain technologies offer promising solutions through secure, immutable ledgers, adoption rates remain low, and extant research focuses primarily on theoretical frameworks lacking empirical substantiation. Addressing this gap, the present study reconceptualises transparency barriers as capability frictions, systematic impediments that prevent firms from effectively deploying sensing, seizing, and transformation capabilities. Through an in-depth case study of a Swedish OEM and its suppliers, four transparency barriers are identified: information inaccuracy, risks of information sharing, lack of communication protocols, and future communications compatibility. Analysis demonstrates how these barriers create capability frictions by weakening sensing through information asymmetry, constraining seizing through limited collaboration, and restricting transformation through weak data governance. The findings reveal how blockchain's distinctive properties, immutability, transparency, and decentralised consensus, systematically reduce these frictions, enabling firms to transition from weakened to enhanced dynamic capabilities. Five propositions are developed theorising the mechanisms through which blockchain serves as a digital enabler for capability transformation, contributing to dynamic capabilities theory and supply chain management practice.

papers.title: Energy- and labour-aware scheduling under uncertainty: a decomposition framework for stochastic batch-processing systems
institutions: University of Applied Sciences Upper Austria
papers.abstract: Motivated by the energy-intensive heat-treatment operations of a European lead-acid battery manufacturer, this study addresses energy- and labour-aware scheduling for a stochastic batch-processing system with waiting-time constraints and programme-compatibility requirements. We formalise the problem as a two-level optimisation decomposed into five sub-decisions and design a generic scheduling framework spanning from simple Rule-Based Heuristics (RH) to rules automatically synthesised by Genetic Programming (GP) for a single sub-decision. All approaches are evaluated in an agent-based discrete-event simulation mirroring the company's production. Optimising all five sub-decisions using handcrafted rules (Best RH) significantly reduces costs by 40.8% at low and 85.4% at high utilisation over Current Practice, with substantially improved solution robustness. Substituting a single sub-decision with GP-evolved rules reveals both what evolved rules achieve alone and what potential handcrafted rules leave. At high utilisation, it yields a significant 41.9% cost reduction over Current Practice, whereas on the already optimised Best RH the cost gain is marginal and non-significant – but robustness still improves markedly, a critical advantage in stochastic environments. The central contribution is methodological: partitioning the problem by decision structure rather than machine structure reduces complexity enough for handcrafted rules to remain competitive with evolved ones.

papers.title: Learning from forecast revisions for inventory replenishment under non-stationary demand
papers.abstract: Forecast revisions contain information about emerging demand changes that is typically discarded in inventory-control policies. Our two main contributions are (i) a POMDP state augmentation that pairs the history of forecast revisions with Bayesian change-point and forecast-uncertainty signals, and (ii) FR-PPO (Forecast Revision Proximal Policy Optimization), a two-level recurrent architecture that encodes this revision history through a GRU inside a RecurrentPPO controller centered on an uncertainty-adjusted base-stock reference. We evaluated FR-PPO against two classical and six reinforcement learning benchmarks in five synthetic demand scenarios and seven regime-active M5 SKUs. FR-PPO is the best PPO-family policy in all five synthetic scenarios and achieves the lowest overall cost on three of them, reducing cost by 72.2% relative to adaptive BaseStock under seasonal demand while reducing adaptation lag by 63%. The method is not uniformly dominant: off-policy SAC baselines retain an advantage under sparse, intermittent demand, delimiting where the revision signal is most valuable. On real M5 data, FR-PPO reduces cost relative to adaptive BaseStock on all seven SKUs (4.2%–23.0%). These findings identify forecast-revision histories as useful, low-cost decision information for replenishment under demand non-stationarity.

papers.title: A systematic review of the collaborative intelligence in multi-agent scheduling
institutions: UiT The Arctic University of Norway
papers.abstract: Traditional scheduling assumes a single actor, while real-world scenarios often involve multiple decision-making units with conflicting objectives, requiring collaboration, coordination, negotiation, and collective intelligence. Multi-agent scheduling (MAS) provides a realistic framework for modelling such interactions under shared resources. This article presents a comprehensive scientometric and systematic review of two-agent and multi-agent scheduling, examining the field’s development paths, knowledge structure, and emerging research clusters. Main path, cluster, and keyword analyses are integrated to trace knowledge diffusion, identify influential studies and research branches, and examine how collaborative intelligence is manifested across scheduling contexts. The findings reveal an evolution from early complexity-oriented single-machine and dual-agent models toward richer production environments, advanced computational methods, and application-oriented MAS in smart manufacturing, energy systems, edge computing, and decentralised project scheduling. More importantly, the synthesis reveals a broader transition from optimizing competing agent-specific objectives toward interaction-driven collaborative scheduling intelligence based on coordination, negotiation, information sharing, adaptation, and collective learning. This domain-level perspective suggests that future MAS should integrate decentralised decision-making, adaptive intelligence, and system-level coordination to reconcile local objectives with system-wide performance.

papers.title: A causal analytics approach for interpretable supply chain risk and supplier performance evaluation
papers.abstract: Traditional machine learning (ML) techniques are widely used to support operational supply chain decisions, but their “black box” nature limits transparency and actionability. This study addresses this challenge by exploring the effectiveness of causal discovery methods and large language models (LLMs) in supply chain management with a focus on the automotive industry. Six causal discovery algorithms- Peter–Clark (PC), Fast Causal Inference (FCI), Greedy Equivalence Search (GES), DirectLiNGAM, NOTEARS, and Regression with Subsequent Independence Test (RESIT) are benchmarked against an expert-validated ground-truth graph constructed from 18 domain experts with a combined 300+ years of experience, using 12 months of internal supplier Key Performance Indicator (KPI) data. RESIT achieves the closest alignment with expert knowledge, with a False Discovery Rate of 0.1429, Structural Hamming Distance of 1, precision and recall of 0.8571 and an F1-score of 0.85, outperforming all other algorithms on every metric. Robustness of the estimated causal effect of Backlog on Escalation is confirmed through three refutation tests- random common cause, random subset and placebo treatment returning high p-values of 0.96, 0.76, and 0.98 respectively, indicating insensitivity to spurious confounders and random perturbations. Counterfactual simulation shows that reducing Backlog by 50%–70% consistently lowers escalation levels across suppliers. LLMs contribute by extracting causal factors from unstructured external event data, accelerating causal graph construction, and reducing dependence on manual expert input. LLM-derived causal graphs are further compared with expert-validated models to ensure alignment and reliability, and are operationalised through a Weighted Sum Model risk score linking external drivers to internal KPIs for actionable supplier escalation decisions.

papers.title: Adaptive disaster relief logistics under uncertainty: a hybrid robust–fuzzy two‑stage mathematical model with inter‑regional sharing
papers.venue: Journal of the Operational Research Society
papers.abstract: Disaster relief logistics presents major challenges. Uncertain demand, scarce resources, disrupted transportation networks, and rapidly evolving conditions make equitable and timely distribution extremely difficult. This paper proposes a hybrid robust-fuzzy two-stage programming framework for the procurement, allocation, and inventory management of essential relief commodities. A rolling horizon approach continuously updates decisions using real-time demand and inventory data, enhancing adaptability and responsiveness. The study makes three key contributions. First, it develops a hybrid robust-fuzzy approach that simultaneously addresses imprecision, incomplete data, and evolving multi-period demand, advancing beyond traditional deterministic and stochastic models. Second, it incorporates coordinated inter-regional sharing and dynamic transshipment of surplus supplies, improving efficiency in humanitarian logistics. Third, it validates the integrated rolling horizon and robust-fuzzy framework through an earthquake case study in Iran, where mountainous terrain and damaged roads intensify mobility challenges. Results show significant reductions in shortages and total cost compared to deterministic and traditional robust approaches. These findings offer actionable insights for policymakers and humanitarian organisations seeking adaptive disaster response systems.

papers.title: Systematic evaluation of TabPFN-TS and Chronos-2 for zero-shot heat load forecasting in district heating networks
papers.abstract: District heating energy hubs require reliable heat load forecasts for efficient operational scheduling. Forecasting models trained on historical data may require retraining as networks evolve. Zero-shot time-series foundation models and in-context forecasting therefore offer a promising alternative: they can adapt at inference time from recent observations rather than by repeated retraining. This study systematically evaluates TabPFN-TS and Chronos-2 for probabilistic heat load forecasting in two German district heating networks and compares them with trained baselines. Of particular interest is whether TabPFN-TS, whose underlying model is pretrained entirely on synthetic tabular rather than time-series data, can capture complex district heating dynamics. We analyze covariate choice, context length, temporal resolution, and forecast horizon on selected operating weeks, evaluate the selected configuration over the full year, and assess cross-network transfer. The principal benchmark assumes perfect weather forecasts; a separate sensitivity analysis uses retrospective weather predictions. Hourly 24-hour forecasting with a 12-week rolling context and ambient temperature provides a parsimonious configuration; longer context windows do not improve accuracy. Both TSFMs outperform all trained baselines in deterministic accuracy in the full-year benchmarks. Chronos-2 achieves the best deterministic scores, with TabPFN-TS remaining close: their CVRMSE values on the main data set are 12.48% and 13.07%, respectively. Chronos-2 also achieves lower continuous ranked probability scores in both networks, with TabPFN-TS remaining close. Finally, a TSFM-based Multi-Resolution Residual-Correction Forecaster combines an hourly base forecast with short-term high-resolution corrections. Relative to direct high-resolution forecasting, it generally reduces errors in total heat demand over 12-hour periods and recorded prediction times.

papers.title: Long-lead forecasting of El Niño–Southern Oscillation using score-driven models with many predictors
papers.abstract: We consider long-lead forecasting of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) climate phenomenon. This is widely seen as a challenging task from a methodological perspective. At the same time, ENSO events are of substantial societal importance. We adopt a class of score-driven models to capture the key dynamic features of the Niño 3.4 index and include a large set of previously designed predictors. We provide details of our forecasting methodology and assess the forecast accuracy for a range of different model specifications and estimation strategies. We conclude that a model with a good description of the dynamic features in the data is also able to provide accurate forecasts for almost all lead times, up to 18 months ahead. The large set of predictors is shown to support the provision of accurate long-range forecasts for specific lead times.

papers.title: Managing geopolitical risk in global supply chains: A qualitative study of European multinational enterprises
institutions: WHU – Otto Beisheim School of Management
papers.abstract: Geopolitical risk has emerged as a major disruptive risk to global supply chains and the operations of multinational enterprises (MNEs) today. Drawing on a qualitative content analysis of the annual reports of 20 European MNEs across five industries, supported by a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline, this study examines how companies strategically manage geopolitical risk in their supply chains. We extend an established supply chain risk framework by conceptualizing geopolitical risk management (GRM) as a distinct strategic risk management dimension centered on reducing geopolitical exposure, in contrast to supply chain risk management (SCRM), which enhances operational resilience within existing supply chain structures. Applying this distinction, we identify seven key GRM strategies, including localization, decentralized procurement and R&D, direct sourcing, supplier diversification, geographical production diversification, circular economy initiatives, and political engagement. Furthermore, applying the Triple-P framework in a disclosure-based setting suggests that companies facing different forms of supply chain complexity across the partnership, product, and process dimensions disclose distinct portfolios of GRM strategies. The findings of this study provide cross-industry insights into the strategic orientation of large European MNEs and support managerial decision making to strengthen resilience in the face of supply chain and geopolitical risk.

papers.title: Agents of collaborative adaptation: modelling temporal resilience in supply chains
papers.abstract: Abstract Supply-chain disruptions vary in intensity, scale, and frequency, producing temporally heterogeneous impacts on network viability. The emphasis on exposure and topology has anchored resilience in network structure, obscuring how collaboration and trust govern its phase-specific temporal dynamics, including resistive capabilities, adaptation speed, containment, and recovery. This study thus develops an agent-based simulation of the Netherlands logistics network, in which nodes operate as autonomous agents that redistribute load under capacity, link, and trust constraints. Cascading failures are simulated with trust-gated, capacity-aware, and collaboration-dependent load reallocation, capturing both immediate contagion and multi-step redistribution dynamics. The framework compares rule-based heuristics with adaptive AI agents trained using supervised imitation, online multiplicative adaptation, and cross-entropy policy search. Temporal resilience is then measured across each phase specific metrics of absorptive, adaptive, and recovery phases across the collaboration structure. This points to the main contribution of this article, in which AI agents improve adaptation and cascade containment through targeted use of high-trust, high-capacity links, while recovery dynamics remain bounded by structural and exogenous constraints. This points to a layered view of resilience, where performance depends on the interaction between network configuration, trust-mediated coordination, and agent-level adaptation.

papers.title: Collaborative routing problems in automated warehouses
papers.abstract: The pick-and-drive system is a novel solution for warehouse automation. It integrates two types of autonomous mobile robots (AMRs). Storage and supply AMRs (S-AMRs) navigate to a storage area, where they lift unit loads and transport them to a disposition area. Picking AMRs (P-AMRs) move freely within this disposition area. They carry bins and meet S-AMRs to collect items from the unit loads attached to the S-AMRs by means of robotic arms. We take an operational perspective on the pick-and-drive system and focus on the problem of determining and scheduling meeting locations and sequences of the AMRs, so that all required items are picked. This setting is interpreted as a vehicle routing problem, where the customers (S-AMRs) collaborate with the vehicles (P-AMRs). We consider two objective functions, minimizing the total distance driven by the AMRs and minimizing the sum of completion times of the P-AMRs. We translate these routing problems into a mathematical framework and provide theoretical insights by examining a specific case where the potential meeting points lie along a line. For this scenario, we present an approximation algorithm for the case of minimizing the overall distance traveled and demonstrate that minimizing the sum of completion times is strongly NP-complete. Additionally, we prove strong NP-completeness of the general case when minimizing the overall distance traveled. Leveraging the structural insights, we develop heuristics that are evaluated in a numerical study. Our results highlight the potential impact of the system in practice.

papers.title: PROSWIN: Probabilistic Solar Wind Speed Forecasting Using Deep Distributional Regression From Solar Images
institutions: Deutsches Zentrum für Luft- und Raumfahrt e. V. (DLR)
papers.abstract: Abstract Accurately predicting fast solar wind conditions is challenging, as uncertainties are large and unquantified by traditional single‐value prediction models. In particular, the risks of high‐speed solar wind streams (HSSs), which can cause damage to technological infrastructure, cannot be reliably assessed without probabilistic forecasts. We present PROSWIN, a probabilistic machine learning model that forecasts the hourly solar wind speed (SWS) at Earth with a 4‐day lead time. The approach combines solar images and magnetograms using a deep neural network coupled to a distributional regression algorithm. Because standard error metrics underweight the relevance of HSS peaks, we further introduce the prediction score (PS) , a model‐selection metric that jointly rewards timeline and HSS peak accuracy. On 14 years of data, our forecast achieves very well‐calibrated uncertainties (<1% average absolute coverage deviation). Using the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), a metric that assesses distributional accuracy, we obtain a timeline CRPS of 41.0 km/s, an HSS peak CRPS of 45.3 km/s, and a PS of 42.3 km/s. We find that the 171 Å channel is an important complement to the typically used 193 and 211 Å channels and that the PS for model selection improves the applicability of the model. Compared to selected models from the literature, ours is the only one that is accurate for both timeline and HSS peak values, rather than trading one off against the other. These results support the advantages of probabilistic over single‐value solar wind models. The introduced methods are also transferable to other forecasting problems.

papers.title: Guest editorial: Advancing the future of retail operations with cutting-edge technologies
papers.venue: International Journal of Physical Distribution & Logistics Management
papers.abstract: The retail industry is fundamentally changing due to emerging technologies (Morenza-Cinos et al., 2019; Ta et al., 2023). Machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) for example, can help retailers improve demand forecasting accuracy (Modgil et al., 2021; Chou et al., 2023) and analyze data in real time, enabling them to better align their inventory decisions with their logistics network capabilities (Sodero et al., 2019). Other technologies such as blockchain, the Internet of Things (IoT) and augmented reality (AR) allow retailers to support product tracking and authenticity verification, real-time data accessibility and product visualization for customers, as well as the automation of processing product returns (Hartley et al., 2021). Furthermore, these technologies have also contributed to the rise of new retail formats and fulfillment models, such as reserve/buy online pick up/return in store, webrooming and buy in store/ship-to-home, which allow retailers to offer a more seamless customer experience across retail channels (Jin et al., 2023). Additionally, last-mile delivery is being reshaped by new delivery modes, including drones and autonomous delivery (Merkert et al., 2022).While these technological innovations offer many opportunities for retailers to improve their operational efficiency, their implementation often poses significant challenges for retailers (Angelopoulos et al., 2023). Adopting new technologies requires substantial financial investments, cross-functional coordination and changes to legacy systems. For example, while over 90% of retailers have adopted AI in some shape or form, often as pilots, most retailers struggle with rolling out this technology on a larger scale [1].Research on omnichannel retailing has shown that integrating physical and digital retail channels can improve customer service experience and convenience. However, it can also create tensions related to inventory visibility, order orchestration and last-mile cost management (Hubner et al., 2016; Melacini et al., 2018). Other technologies, such as IoT and blockchain, promise greater supply chain traceability and transparency. Yet these benefits often depend on system-wide participation and sustained investments from supply chain partners (Hartley et al., 2022). Moreover, work on data-driven retail processes suggests that these tools are only as effective as the underlying data quality and managerial capabilities that support their use (Sodero et al., 2019; Modgil et al., 2021). As such, the successful implementation of these technologies is highly dependent on foundational organizational processes and managerial capabilities.In addition to implementation issues, retailers struggle with fully realizing the promised and expected benefits associated with these emerging technologies. Research suggests that the performance outcomes of these emerging technologies are contingent on contextual factors such as retail format, product and service characteristics, channel configuration, customer expectations and retailers’ digital maturity (Gauri et al., 2021; Castelo-Branco et al., 2022). For instance, technologies designed to enrich customer experience, such as AR and other digital engagement tools, may improve customers’ purchase confidence and product evaluation. However, they might also generate limited value or even friction if they are poorly aligned with customer needs or retail channel design (Grewal and Roggeveen, 2020; Hilken et al., 2017; Poushneh and Vasquez-Parraga, 2017). Technologies designed to enhance fulfillment, such as automated delivery systems or autonomous solutions, can reduce lead time and expand service options, but they also introduce operational complexities, regulatory concerns and cost tradeoffs that might offset their benefits (Merkert et al., 2022). While prior work has enhanced our understanding of how emerging technologies have the potential to continue to transform retail operations and the customer experience, much of this work remains conceptual in nature or limited in scope (Guida et al., 2023; Modgil et al., 2022).The understanding of drivers, implementation issues and outcomes of technology adoption in retail operations varies significantly depending on the technology under investigation. For example, implementation issues related to AI or big data vary greatly from those related to IoT technologies which focus on enabling real-time monitoring and connectivity across supply chain and in-store operations. Similarly, the discussion of automation versus human input varies tremendously across these technologies. Thus, the diversity of technological contexts underscores the need for context-specific research investigations in order to offer in-depth insights into how specific technologies are implemented in the retail industry.Against this backdrop this special issue is positioned at the intersection of retail operations and emerging technologies. It seeks to explore the drivers to the adoption of these technologies, the considerations that shape their implementation and the ways in which the combination of these elements can redefine customer experience and, ultimately, reshape the industry.In this editorial we first introduce the six manuscripts included in the special issue, highlighting how each manuscript advances our understanding of how retailers engage in the adoption of these technologies, technology-specific implementation opportunities and challenges and retail, consumer and supply chain outcomes. Second, we identify avenues for future research structured around the three key dimensions of antecedents, implementation opportunities and challenges and outcomes. In doing so, this editorial provides a starting point for additional research to further explore the impacts of emerging technologies in retail operations while also encouraging research that is theoretically grounded and empirically rigorous.Employing a diverse set of empirical methods ranging from qualitative and survey to simulation and quantitative techniques, the six papers in this special issue collectively portray retail technology not as a set of isolated innovations, but as an interconnected ecosystem in which operational design, consumer behavior, organizational capabilities and channel integration jointly determine value creation. Across the studies, a common theme emerges: the success of emerging retail technologies depends not merely on technical feasibility, but on how effectively technologies are embedded within broader omnichannel systems and aligned with consumer expectations, organizational capabilities and strategic objectives. Yuan et al. (2026) challenge the assumption that omnichannel return strategies such as buy-online-return-in-store (BORIS) automatically create value, demonstrating that their benefits are highly conditional and dependent on complementary operational and marketing decisions. Garg et al. (2026) similarly show that the viability of drone delivery hinges not only on operational efficiency, but also on consumer motivation, perceived value and retailer-consumer engagement. Complementarily, Merkert et al. (2026) explore how drones can enhance warehousing and last-mile delivery from an organizational perspective and highlight barriers as well as opportunities for the implementation of this technology. Park et al. (2026) further extend this ecosystem perspective by illustrating how third-party delivery platforms can complement, rather than cannibalize, retailers’ proprietary channels when channel integration is strategically managed. Oliveira et al. (2026) shift attention toward the information-processing capabilities required to coordinate increasingly decentralized and consumer-centric fulfillment systems, while Bianco et al. (2026) demonstrate that warehouse automation creates value only when developed as a dynamic organizational capability aligned with evolving retail complexity. Collectively, these studies build a broader picture of modern retail transformation in which technology adoption, channel coordination, organizational adaptability and consumer engagement operate as mutually reinforcing components of a highly integrated retail ecosystem. A summary of the selected papers is presented in Table 1.Yuan et al. (2026) examine the role of BORIS as a popular strategy to attract consumers. In this study, the authors analyze data gathered for North America’s Top 1,000 e-retailers (2013–2019). They reveal that BORIS’s operational challenges often outweigh its benefits. Analyzing website sales, conversion rates, order value and traffic, this study shows that BORIS offers negligible direct benefits for pure e-retailers. For omnichannel “bricks-and-clicks” retailers, BORIS only weakly boosts traffic and order value when paired with free return shipping or low sponsored search spend, though it can drive incremental traffic when synchronized with high-spend search campaigns. Ultimately, their findings suggest that while BORIS can offer highly specific, conditional advantages, its overall impact on e-retailer performance is weak, challenging the conventional wisdom of its effectiveness.Garg et al. (2026) shift the conversation on drone-enabled retail operations away from purely technical and operational feasibility toward a deeper understanding of the demand side. The research offers a timely and theoretically rigorous examination of a critical bottleneck in retail innovation: the formation of consumer motivation. Drawing on expectancy theory and integrating partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with Necessary Condition Analysis (NCA), the research provides a dual perspective on what is “sufficient” to drive motivation and what is “indispensable” for it to exist. The findings show that unless consumers perceive meaningful personal benefit, improvements in technical reliability (expectancy) or outcome utility (instrumentality) are unlikely to generate the necessary motivational force for adoption. The paper further enriches the retail conversation by introducing Consumer Engagement with Retailers (CER) as a critical relational mechanism in technology acceptance.Merkert et al. (2026) adopt a qualitative research approach to shed light on the technological, organizational and environmental factors that impact drone operations for warehousing and last-mile delivery. The authors conduct semi-structured interviews with 38 warehouse and drone delivery managers across the globe to explore the organizational challenges and limitations associated with the implementation of this new technology for fulfillment operations. Analyzing the data through the lens of Technology–Organization–Environment (TOE), the findings not only highlight the benefits and barriers of drone delivery adoption but also the importance of inter-organizational collaboration and different governance mechanisms for successful implementation of the technology.Park et al. (2026) examine the synergy between consumer-facing delivery platforms and omnichannel retail operations. Drawing on channel capabilities theory and leveraging a proprietary dataset, the authors show that platform partnerships can complement rather than cannibalize retailers’ direct channels. Specifically, each platform partnership increases physical store sales by 1.36% and direct online sales by 42.6%, suggesting that third-party platforms function as effective customer acquisition and discovery mechanisms that redirect traffic to higher-margin proprietary channels. The benefits are particularly pronounced for restaurant chains with sparse physical networks and for firms with deeper channel integration, where customers order through the retailer’s own interface while the platform handles fulfillment. Overall, the study demonstrates that strategic collaboration with delivery platforms can expand, rather than substitute for, direct-channel sales.Oliveira et al. (2026) focus on how omnichannel retailers can shift away from centralized fulfillment models toward distribution networks that are both adaptive and consumer-centric. Drawing on Organizational Information Processing Theory (OIPT), the authors argue that coordinating multiple delivery modes (quick commerce, scheduled delivery and in-store pickup) across varied consumer demands generates considerable task uncertainty and information load. This challenge is amplified in emerging markets, where security concerns make attended home deliveries the norm and tight time-window coordination a common operational constraint. Using data from a Brazilian omnichannel retailer and a consumer survey, they conduct simulation analyses to test whether an adaptive network that allocates orders in real time according to inventory availability and consumer preferences can mitigate this task uncertainty. Their results show that no single facility type can effectively serve such diverse demands. A decentralized, hybrid configuration that postpones fulfillment decisions through real-time data instead reduces task uncertainty and lowers failed delivery attempts, while also cutting quick-commerce fulfillment times. Ultimately, the study illustrates how information-processing capabilities help empower omnichannel retailers to manage operational tradeoffs in increasingly consumer-centric environments.Finally, Bianco et al. (2026) examine how grocery retailers implement warehouse automation to transform logistics processes in response to operational complexity. They argue that warehouse automation is a dynamic capability rather than a technical investment. Specifically, the authors analyze core distribution processes by conducting semi-structured interviews with eight automation providers and six grocery retailers, complemented by site visits. Their results unveil five strategic dimensions that guide warehouse automation decisions: selectivity, accessibility, expandability, scalability and resilience. Interpreted through the lens of Dynamic Capabilities theory (Teece et al., 1997), their framework demonstrates that selectivity and accessibility strengthen a firm’s sensing capabilities for effective decision-making, while expandability and scalability facilitate seizing new business opportunities. They conclude that successful automation depends on managerial and organizational logic that aligns technological design with evolving retail demands, bridging the gap between functional intralogistics research and capability-based strategic perspectives.This section develops an integrative research agenda organized around three interrelated dimensions: the antecedents of technology adoption, the implementation and operational integration of these technologies, and their outcomes and systemic implications. papers.title: Optimizing freight rail electrification: A framework for charge station selection and battery charge/swap scheduling
papers.venue: Transportation Research Part E Logistics and Transportation Review
papers.abstract: Battery-electric freight trains are promising for decarbonization by providing zero-emission transportation alternatives. Successful adoption of battery-electric freight trains depends on an efficient electrification strategy, involving infrastructure setup and charging scheduling. The study presents a comprehensive model for the optimal design of charging infrastructure and charge scheduling for trains. To provide greater recharging flexibility, we allow a battery to be either charged or swapped at a deployed station, and each train can carry multiple batteries. This problem is formulated as a mixed-integer linear programming model with a Rectangle Piecewise Linear Approximation (PLA) technique. To obtain strategic and tactical solutions, we develop two algorithms to solve the optimization problem: (1) a Fix Algorithm (FA), and (2) Benders Decomposition (BD) algorithm with extra feasibility cuts to speed up the procedure. In computational experiments, we use the original model with the PLA technique, and the two proposed algorithms. Statistical analysis verifies the modified BD algorithm with extra feasibility cuts performs best with respect to the objective function value in larger instances, closely followed by FA, and the PLA technique provides the least optimal solutions. Specifically, compared with the standard BD, the modified BD can reduce the objective function value by 11.73%, 30.92% and 51.58% on large, extra large and high-frequency instances, respectively. Sensitivity analysis is implemented to investigate the impact of delay penalty weight, charge rate, demand pattern and battery inventory. Finally, a case study is conducted to demonstrate the application of the proposed framework in a representative freight rail planning setting.

papers.title: Exact and metaheuristic approaches for a real-world discrete lot-sizing and scheduling problem in the automotive industry
papers.abstract: We address a production scheduling problem arising in the seat manufacturing auto industry, characterised by multiple racetracks and a wide variety of car models. The challenge is to determine the optimal sequence of molds to mount on each racetrack to maintain inventory levels within target ranges while minimising changeovers. To tackle this, we formulate a mixed-integer programming model evaluated using Gurobi. Additionally, we develop a Greedy Randomised Adaptive Search Procedure (GRASP) to provide a practical, non-commercial alternative. The GRASP incorporates two specialised local search procedures: the first achieves feasibility by reducing shortages, and the second aims to minimise changeovers. Computational experiments on 133 real-world instances demonstrate the merit of our approaches. The exact MIP solver proves optimality in under 30 seconds on average. Given the same 30-second budget, GRASP achieves a 2.42% average deviation, which is equivalent to fewer than a single additional changeover, finding 77% of global optima. Extending the runtime to the 5-minute company limit reduces deviation to 1.65%. Most importantly, compared to the historical manual baseline, this approach reduces tool changeovers by nearly 50%, resulting in estimated annual savings of $250,000 per plant.

papers.title: Supply chain risk identification using AI-powered topic modelling: implications for demand forecasting in oil and gas companies
papers.venue: Journal of the Operational Research Society
papers.abstract: The oil and gas industry is highly exposed to political, economic, and supply–demand disruptions, making early risk identification critical for supply chain performance. This study applies AI-enabled topic modelling to extract risk indicators from large unstructured datasets and integrates them into gasoline demand forecasting models, showing how qualitative risk signals can improve uncertainty management in supply chains. Building on these insights, the paper proposes a generalisable three-stage methodological framework that formalises the pipeline from automated text-based risk identification through forecast validation to short-term operational adjustment. In this context, short-term operational adjustments include tactical changes to procurement, inventory levels, production scheduling, logistics routeing, and short-term hedging decisions made in response to risk-aware demand and volatility forecasts. The framework’s principal methodological contribution lies in operationalising AI-enabled text analytics within real-world supply chain planning processes through a formally specified decision-flow model. Results from the empirical validation on a 15-year gasoline demand dataset show that incorporating text-derived risk indicators, selected via rigorous feature selection, improves both point-forecast accuracy and density-forecast calibration relative to naive and seasonal baselines, offering transferable guidance for policymakers and industry stakeholders seeking to strengthen energy system resilience.

papers.title: Navigating the exploitation–exploration paradox: the impact of industry 4.0 technologies on supply chain performance from the Organisational ambidexterity lens
papers.abstract: Industry 4.0 (I4.0) technologies have significant potential to improve supply chain performance, yet organisations often struggle to realise these benefits in practice. Drawing on Structural Ambidexterity Theory, this study examines how specific I4.0 technologies affect core supply chain functions, identifies the principal barriers to implementation, and explores how organisational and sectoral characteristics influence implementation success. The study conducted 19 semi-structured interviews with supply chain directors, digital transformation leaders, and I4.0 consultants across the automotive, pharmaceutical, food and beverage, construction, and high-technology manufacturing sectors. Data were analysed using a three-stage thematic coding process (open, axial, and selective coding) anchored in Simsek et al. (Citation2009) partitional ambidexterity framework. The findings reveal that different I4.0 technologies generate distinct impacts across supply chain functions. Base technologies, including IoT, sensors, machine learning-driven forecasting, robotics, and big data analytics, deliver measurable improvements in demand planning, inventory management, manufacturing operations, and logistics through enhanced visibility, automation, and operational efficiency. In contrast, advanced technologies such as AI-driven decision intelligence, digital twins, simulation, and augmented reality offer greater transformative potential but require substantially higher levels of organisational learning, experimentation, and integration capability. The study further identifies five interconnected implementation barriers: process immaturity, legacy system integration challenges, human resistance to change, workforce capability gaps, and investment uncertainty. Organisational culture, leadership commitment, firm size, and sector-specific regulatory and competitive conditions are found to shape the success and pace of I4.0 adoption. Building on these findings, the study argues that I4.0 adoption creates a fundamental socio-technical tension between exploitation and exploration. Structural separation of exploitative and explorative technology initiatives, enabled through cloud computing and big data analytics, emerges as a viable mechanism for managing this tension. The study extends the partitional ambidexterity framework through the concept of Connected Partitioning and introduces Virtual Integration as a digital mechanism linking differentiated capability streams. It further proposes Structural Buffering as a mechanism for protecting explorative technology initiatives from the socio-technical resistance concentrated in that domain, and identifies a sequential ambidexterity pathway in which exploitative stabilisation is a precondition for explorative capability. The research provides a theoretically grounded and empirically rich understanding of I4.0-enabled supply chain transformation and offers actionable guidance for managers navigating digital transformation initiatives.

papers.title: A Robust Fuzzy Optimization Framework for Circular Supply Chain Network Design under Uncertainty
papers.abstract: Circular supply chain network design requires not only the coordination of forward and reverse networks but also an explicit representation of how products are manufactured, recovered, and reintegrated across multiple life cycles. However, many existing models often treat manufacturing and recycling in an aggregated manner, limiting their ability to capture operational circularity, particularly under uncertainty. This study proposes a multi-period, multi-product network design model for circular supply chains that integrates forward and reverse bill of materials with manufacturing and recycling process networks. The model jointly optimizes facility locations, technology choices, capacity levels, and commodity flows. Uncertainties in product demand, material supply, return rates, returned product quality, and economic parameters are represented using fuzzy numbers to capture epistemic uncertainty when reliable probability distributions are difficult to establish. A modified hybrid robust possibilistic chance-constrained programming approach is developed using possibility and credibility measures, together with a linearization scheme to ensure consistency in feasibility degrees. The applicability of the model is demonstrated through a lead-acid battery supply chain case study, followed by comparative and sensitivity analyses. Under deterministic conditions, the integrated circular network obtains a 7.68% reduction in total cost compared with the linear network. Furthermore, an evaluation across different uncertainty realizations shows that the proposed robust fuzzy approach obtains lower average total cost and standard deviations than its conventional fuzzy and deterministic counterparts. These results demonstrate the potential of the proposed framework in improving cost efficiency and solution stability while supporting strategic circular supply chain decisions under uncertainty.

papers.title: Monte Carlo tree search for the multi-crane scheduling problem with temporal constraints
institutions: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Abstract This study addresses the multi-crane scheduling problem with temporal constraints (MCSPTC) arising in steelmaking shops, where multiple rail-guided overhead cranes transport materials on shared tracks and must strictly avoid interference. The problem requires jointly determining task assignment and sequencing decisions while satisfying temporal constraints on task start times, including time windows and precedence relations. In practice, manufacturing execution system data are updated frequently, requiring high quality solutions to be generated repeatedly within short computation times. However, existing heuristics lack quality guarantees, while exact models do not scale to industrial-size instances within practical time limits. To tackle these challenges, we formulate the MCSPTC as a sequential decision process and propose a Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS)–based solution framework. The proposed approach performs look-ahead planning at each decision point using a schedule construction mechanism. To improve search efficiency, we develop a feasibility-based action pruning strategy that eliminates actions inevitably leading to infeasible schedules prior to node expansion. We further tailor the value backup and final action selection rules to account for the tight temporal feasibility and the varying size of the feasible action space induced by temporal constraints. Our numerical results suggest that the proposed MCTS framework yields better solutions than existing heuristics within short computation times. In particular, the proposed method improves upon the heuristic baselines by approximately 5%–7% for both small and medium-scale instances within one minute and large-scale instances within about three minutes.

papers.title: An energy-efficient coordinated procurement, production, and batch delivery scheduling system for sustainable operations with Net-Zero emissions
papers.venue: Transportation Research Part E Logistics and Transportation Review
institutions: Ahsanullah University of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Over the last decade, rising energy prices, global warming, the harmful effects of energy use, and carbon emissions have highlighted the importance of energy and carbon efficiency. In response to local energy regulations and carbon-sensitive markets, manufacturers and logistics organizations are actively seeking effective methods to improve energy and carbon efficiency. This research enhances supply chain planning and scheduling by combining procurement, production, and delivery decisions to support sustainable operations through simultaneously optimizing costs, energy consumption, and carbon emissions. An E nergy- E fficient C oordinated P roduction- D istribution S ystem ( EE-CPDS ) is designed, accounting for a flexible job-shop scheduling environment with inter-machine transport times and sequence-dependent setup times to reflect real production configurations. To address the computational challenge, we propose a novel multi-objective adaptive search memetic algorithm (MOASMA) that outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of solution quality, i.e., generating global solutions closer to true Pareto front with average hypervolume (HV) value of 0.7131 and Inverted Generational Distance Plus (IGD + ) value of 0.0249 across nine test instances, which is further endorsed by nonparametric statistical analysis. Among the instances solved by all competing algorithms, MOASMA provides better solutions for 77% of them. The correctness and effectiveness of the developed algorithm are verified by comparing the results with an exact solver (Gurobi), which is effective for small and medium-sized instances, while MOASMA proves efficient for larger-scale problems. The proposed system and algorithm will assist enterprises in solving practical-sized instances while rationalizing coordinated procurement, production, and distribution decisions that support sustainable operations and drive progress toward net-zero emissions.

papers.title: A stochastic decision analytics framework for hydrogen refueling infrastructure planning in sustainable freight supply chains
papers.abstract: The transition toward low-carbon freight transportation requires coordinated planning of hydrogen production, refueling infrastructure, and freight-service operations under substantial technological, economic, and policy uncertainty. In this study, we develop a risk-averse, multi-period stochastic mixed-integer linear programming framework for planning hydrogen refueling infrastructure along freight corridors. Our proposed model jointly determines station-opening schedules, capacity investments, hydrogen production and supply by technology, hydrogen freight adoption, diesel fallback, and emission-policy compliance. We utilize the Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) approach to limit exposure to unfavorable high-cost scenarios involving uncertain freight demand, hydrogen availability, operating costs, and carbon-policy conditions. We demonstrate the applicability of the proposed framework on a U.S. Midwest freight-corridor case study. The optimal base-case solution opens 9 of 12 candidate stations and increases hydrogen adoption in the Base scenario from 12.7% in 2026 to 87.3% in 2035. Annual Base-scenario emissions decrease from 90.4 to 37.1 kt CO 2 e, representing a 58.9% reduction. Compared with the risk-neutral solution, the CVaR-based plan increases the number of opened stations from 8 to 9 and reduces the high-cost tail exposure by $19.3 million. Our sensitivity analysis further shows that clean hydrogen availability and early investment flexibility have stronger effects on emission compliance and tail-risk reduction than carbon pricing alone. We believe that our findings provide guidance and decision support for policymakers, infrastructure developers, hydrogen suppliers, and freight carriers seeking to coordinate resilient and lower-carbon freight-corridor investments.

papers.title: A sustainability-aware optimization framework for port-hinterland truck scheduling
papers.abstract: Abstract Ports are critical gateways for trade and regional growth but also generate substantial externalities such as emissions, congestion, and safety risks. Growing maritime transport and port throughput intensify long-haul diesel truck traffic on hinterland access roads, causing peak-hour bottlenecks, long queues, and higher environmental impacts. Despite many proposed operational strategies, these challenges remain insufficiently addressed. This paper develops a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model for sustainable port-hinterland truck scheduling within an integrated chassis-based remote gate (CRG) and battery-electric trucks (BET) framework for short-haul transport. Using a major UK port case study with real traffic data, the model minimizes total logistics costs, including fixed investments, transport, waiting and idling times for short- and long-haul trucks, and $$\hbox {CO}_2$$ CO 2 emissions. To handle large-scale instances, a two-stage adaptive genetic algorithm (TS-AGA) is proposed and benchmarked against the MILP and a two-stage simulated annealing approach. Collaborative and non-collaborative scheduling strategies are compared to assess the benefits of coordinated decision-making. Results show that collaborative scheduling reduces total system costs by about 13.6% by better synchronizing long-haul diesel truck arrivals with short-haul battery-electric truck operations. Sensitivity analysis further examines how long-haul travel-time uncertainty affects congestion and economic performance. Overall, the proposed MILP model and TS-AGA solution approach demonstrate that coordinated truck scheduling can substantially improve the operational efficiency and sustainability of CRG-BET-based port-hinterland systems. By jointly optimizing long-haul and short-haul operations under collaborative and uncertainty-aware strategies, the study offers a practical and scalable scheduling methodology to reduce logistics costs, congestion, and emissions while supporting sustainable port-city connectivity.
